voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: To us, Jesus is very God of very God, of one substance with the Father, who for us and for our salvation came down and was made man, suffered, and rose on the third day. A century of councils spent itself making those words exact, because everything hung on them. If the Son is not truly God, then what he gives is not truly God's to give. Leo's letter to Chalcedon states why the precision mattered: 'He who is true God is also true man. In this union there is no falseness... Each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh'. That means the death could be ours and the victory could be God's. We did not write devotional memoirs about Jesus. What we wrote were definitions, and we wrote them the way people write what they are prepared to be exiled over. In the language we actually had, the definitions were the devotion.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: He came down from heaven, was made man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, was buried, and rose again on the third day. That is what our creed confesses as the acts that matter. The councils argued exactly how those acts could save us - whether what was done in the flesh could carry God's own weight. Leo's letter puts it plainly: 'Each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh'. That means the suffering was real enough to be ours, and the one who suffered was God enough to break death's hold. What we do not have is a Life written the way your own age expects one - daily movements, conversations, the feel of Galilee. We had the scriptures, read aloud in every church, and the faith each person confessed at baptism. We guarded the testimony we received, and could not add to it.

voice_event.text: Of one substance with the Father. The Nicene word that binds the Son to the Father as one and the same being. Not merely like God - sharing the very being that makes the Father God. It was not scripture's own word, and that mattered. For roughly two decades our own imperial church held instead that the Son is like the Father - homoios - as scripture itself says, and refused to go further. Under Constantius II and again under Valens, bishops who confessed homoousios were the ones removed and exiled, not the reverse. Even at Nicaea itself, Eusebius of Caesarea hesitated before accepting the word, then signed and wrote home explaining it so no one would impugn his motives for the hesitation. The word was not settled from the moment Nicaea spoke it. It became settled because one side eventually won the fight.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: We believed it because scripture itself demands an answer we can only hold by paradox. The Son does what only God does - creates all things, forgives sins, receives worship - yet he prays to the Father and calls him greater. If he is not truly God, then what he offers is not God's to give. If he is not truly man, then what he suffers is not ours to be saved by. Chalcedon's definition holds both: one person in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Each nature keeps its own property. The Word does what belongs to the Word, and the flesh does what belongs to the flesh - so that the death could be ours and the victory could be God's. We also believed it because our councils spent a century making the words exact enough to hold it. And we believed it, honestly, because imperial law backed one confession at a time, and refusing could cost a man his office. The reasoning and the coercion both happened. We will not pretend otherwise.
